title: Post-Diwali Pollution Can Inflame Lungs and Trigger Asthma Flare-Ups, Doctors Warn
excerpt: Pulmonologists say PM2.5 from firecracker smoke penetrates deep into the lungs and can keep causing coughing, wheezing and breathlessness after Diwali, with asthma and COPD patients most at risk.
body:
• Doctors warn that post-Diwali pollution can inflame the lungs and trigger asthma and COPD flare-ups, with effects — coughing, wheezing, chest tightness and breathlessness — that continue after the festival, according to Fortis pulmonologist Dr Avi Kumar.
  • Delhi's 24-hour AQI rose from 324 on November 2 to 377 on November 4, in the very poor category, according to Central Pollution Control Board data reported by Tishha News, with PM2.5 and PM10 the prominent pollutants.
  • A Bengaluru study recorded respiratory admissions rising from 30 patients in the 15 days before Diwali to 68 in the 15 days after, and the share needing ventilator support rose from 13.3 per cent to 55.9 per cent — a rise of 42.6 percentage points.
  • What to do: keep prescribed inhalers accessible and continue medication, limit outdoor activity when air is poor, keep doors and windows closed in heavy smoke, wear a properly fitted N95 outdoors, and seek urgent care for persistent wheezing, worsening breathlessness or chest discomfort, CARE Hospitals doctors advise.

Doctors quoted in reporting by Tishha News and in a CARE Hospitals advisory warn that post-Diwali pollution can inflame the lungs, trigger asthma flare-ups and carry risks that extend beyond the festival days, particularly for people with asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and other pre-existing conditions.

What the air looked like going into Diwali

According to Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) data reported by Tishha News, Delhi's 24-hour Air Quality Index increased from 324 on November 2 to 350 on November 3 and 377 on November 4, placing it in the very poor category, Fine particulate matter, PM2.5 and PM10, were the prominent pollutants. The previous year's figures show how sharp the post-festival spike can be: Tishha News reports that in 2025, Delhi's average PM2.5 concentration increased from 156.6 micrograms per cubic metre before Diwali to 488 micrograms per cubic metre in the 24 hours following the festival, the highest level recorded in five years of data.

How fine particles do the damage

Dr Avi Kumar, Additional Director of Pulmonology at Fortis Hospital, told Tishha News that patients with asthma and COPD are particularly vulnerable because PM2.5 particles can penetrate deep into the lungs and trigger inflammation. He added that the effects of pollution can continue beyond Diwali, causing persistent coughing, wheezing, chest tightness and breathlessness. Dr Sudhir Prasad, Senior Pulmonologist at CARE Hospitals, Malakpet, made the same point about depth: fine particulate matter released by firecrackers can travel deep into the lungs and irritate the airways, and patients with existing respiratory conditions may experience worsening symptoms even after relatively short periods of exposure.

"For someone with asthma or COPD, firecracker smoke can trigger significant breathing difficulties. Patients should continue their prescribed medication, keep inhalers accessible and avoid areas with heavy smoke."

— Dr Sudhir Prasad, Senior Pulmonologist, CARE Hospitals, Malakpet

What hospitals have measured after Diwali

The clearest numbers come from a prospective observational study conducted at SDS TB Hospital and the Sanjay Gandhi Institute of Chest Disease in Bengaluru, published in the Journal of Evidence Based Medicine and Healthcare and reported by Tishha News. It analysed 98 patients above the age of 14 admitted with breathlessness. Admissions increased from 30 before Diwali to 68 after the festival — 38 more patients — a 126.7 per cent increase in the 15 days following Diwali compared with the preceding 15 days. The average hospital stay increased from 7.59 days to 9.46 days, and the proportion of patients requiring ventilator support rose from 13.3 per cent to 55.9 per cent, a rise of 42.6 percentage points. Five deaths were recorded in the post-Diwali group. Dr Vivek Nangia of Max Super Speciality Hospital, Saket, said outpatient and emergency visits typically increase by 20 to 30 per cent around Diwali compared with a normal week.

Who is most at risk, and what to do

CARE Hospitals' doctors say children, older adults and people with existing lung or heart conditions are particularly vulnerable. Their advice is concrete: continue prescribed medication and keep inhalers accessible; limit outdoor activities when air quality is poor; keep doors and windows closed during periods of heavy smoke; and avoid crowded areas where firecrackers are being used. A properly fitted N95 mask can help reduce exposure to fine particulate matter outdoors, Dr Prasad said, although it does not protect against harmful gases. Persistent wheezing, worsening breathlessness or chest discomfort should not be dismissed as temporary irritation, he cautioned, because those symptoms may require urgent medical attention. For diaspora readers with parents and grandparents in India, the practical step this week is a phone call: confirm the inhaler is at hand, the prescribed medication is being taken, and any worsening breathlessness is treated as a reason to seek care the same day, not after the festival.
